issues.item: Triggers: Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly
issues.explanation: For a 56-year-old combat pilot whose index trauma is a life-threatening accident, the trigger set is dominated by bodily-state cues (dizziness, feeling ill), which fits accident-related threat. 'Other people expressing anger, even calmly' points instead toward an interpersonal/assault schema and is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, especially given the absence of other social-conflict or perpetrator-related items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: 'People are not what they seem' implies pervasive interpersonal mistrust. In this profile, the appraisals otherwise center on emotional deadness and a shattered worldview after accident trauma. Strong distrust of others is possible, but here it lacks support from the trigger/threat/memory pattern and feels mismatched with a non-interpersonal accident presentation.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm' conflicts with the rest of the threat profile, which is strongly hypervigilant and danger-sensitive (body on alert, startle to movement) and with avoidance-based coping. While some trauma survivors do engage in risk taking, this specific item sits awkwardly in a profile otherwise organized around fear, somatic triggering, and withdrawal, without corroborating disinhibition or anger-driven strategies.

vignette: Thomas, a 56‑year‑old combat pilot, has spent most of his adult life flying the night sky with the precision of a seasoned navigator. In the spring of 2013, during a routine training sortie over the Pacific, an unexpected engine failure forced a rapid, uncontrolled roll. The aircraft burst into flame as one wing hit the sky, and Thomas, who had survived the crash, was left with a shattered shoulder, a fractured collarbone, and a lingering vertigo that made him feel light‑headed whenever he sat still. The memory of the crackling explosion—the very same sound that now echoes in his mind whenever a sudden bang rings through the cabin—continues to haunt him. Each time that metallic roar returns, Thomas feels his body tighten, his heart pound, and his legs buckle under the weight of a world that seems perpetually on the brink of disaster. The dizziness, the physical unease that follows it, and the jarring sounds of explosions have become the three primary triggers that keep his nervous system on constant alert. They force him to retreat from hospitals and any medical examination, to quit the social gatherings that once filled his evenings, and to adopt a rigid diet in an effort to feel some semblance of control. In the moments of that crash, Thomas had believed the world was a safe place, but the sudden loss of that faith left his beliefs shattered and his perception of danger amplified. The relentless sense of imminent threat—his body on alert, his tendency to startle at the slightest movement, and the compulsive need to scan every corner of his surroundings—only intensifies as he recalls the crash. That same sense of threat spills over into his day‑to‑day life; a faint noise in the kitchen can set off a surge of hypervigilance, and the very act of breathing feels like a gamble against an unseen danger. These negative appraisals are not idle thoughts. Thomas has come to believe that the world is a hostile place where nothing is safe, and that belief fuels his avoidance. He has stopped engaging in activities that once gave him pleasure, from attending his wife’s ballet performances to playing the piano he learned as a child. Every time he feels a tremor of dizziness or hears an unexpected bang, he rationalizes that he must not expose himself to anything that might prompt a medical response. The avoidance extends to his diet; he now watches the composition of every meal, counting portions and restricting foods that might upset his stomach, because the thought of a stomach upset is terrifying. In these moments, the sense of danger is reinforced: by refusing to visit a hospital after a minor bruise, he convinces himself that medical settings are the most hostile environments, and this feeds back into his belief that the world is a dangerous place. His belief that the world is dangerous also sharpens his sensitivity to the triggers: the dizziness and the explosive sounds feel more vivid because they resonate with the conviction that anything could be fatal. The threat he feels also drives his avoidance. After the crash, Thomas has been reluctant to fly even for routine training missions, fearing that another explosion might erupt in the cockpit. The mere presence of an aircraft engine’s whirring sound can make his chest tighten so much he has to leave the flight line early. He now limits his time on the flight deck to short check‑in periods, shutting down the console after a few minutes of monitoring. That reduction in exposure to flying not only fuels his sense of threat but also reinforces his belief that the world is dangerous, because he has chosen to stay away from a place that once defined his identity. Each avoidance strategy, in turn, deepens his negative appraisals. By refusing medical attention, Thomas feels increasingly numb; the lack of professional reassurance compounds his emotional numbness. The emotional deadness he reports now—“I feel dead inside” as he sits alone after a long day—feeds back into his belief that the world has taken everything from him. The more he avoids, the more he believes the world is hostile, and the more he feels detached from himself. He has become convinced that the only way to avoid danger is to keep himself isolated from the very things that might trigger an emergency. Avoidance also keeps his triggers alive. When Thomas denies a medical examination after a slight cut, the uncertainty that follows makes the cut feel more serious, and the dizziness that accompanies the thought of blood feels like a genuine threat. He finds himself more likely to feel dizzy in the mornings because the anxiety about whether he should go to the doctor lingers in the back of his mind. Likewise, the constant sense of threat that keeps him on edge amplifies his avoidance of any situation that might remind him of the crash, from the simple act of driving to the loud rumble of a passing truck. Today, Thomas has decided to seek help. He is afraid that his avoidance will eventually make him incapable of flying, that he will lose his professional identity and his marriage. He hopes that through therapy he can untangle the cycle that keeps his body on constant alert, reclaim the sense of safety that he once took for granted, and finally feel whole again.
